title: Mohnish Pabrai's Interview at Morningstar, The Investor's Mind on December 1, 2023
summary: A personal, psychology-focused interview with Morningstar's Larissa Fernand recorded days after Charlie Munger's death. Pabrai explains Buffett's 'harsh grader' filter for people, how his father's bankruptcies shaped his focus on downside and avoidance of leverage, how the GFC took his net worth from $84M to under $20M and forced Dakshana to shrink its 2009 batch to 50 kids, and the 'rope out of the well' spreadsheet. He closes with Munger's forward-looking habit, the inner scorecard, the $2,000 industrial-psychologist test that mapped his inner self, and his deliberate practice of increasing whatever makes him happy.

ideas.idea: He has a very low emotional response to most events, a hard-coded trait that is an advantage in business and investing.
ideas.detail: Who we are is fixed by genetics and the first five or six years of life; he became aware of this only when others held up a mirror, and it also has disadvantages in life.

ideas.idea: Be a harsh, unfair grader of people: bring the 4 in 100 who impress you into your inner circle and discard the other 96, including the 92 you cannot form an opinion about.
ideas.detail: Buffett told him at their lunch that he is not a great judge of people; in a cocktail party of 100 he could identify only 4 exceptional and 4 arrogant turnoffs. With near-infinite good people on Earth there is no penalty for excluding a good one but a big penalty for including a bad one. Since moving to Austin two years ago he met ~30 people one-on-one and only one became a good friend.

ideas.idea: Ego and arrogance are the natural filter; judge people by how they treat those three or four levels below them, who their friends are, and how they spend their time.
ideas.detail: People put up fronts that a short meeting cannot always penetrate, but to the extent you can see past them it is very helpful. Fairness gets in the way of being the best version of yourself.

ideas.idea: His father pushed him at 25 to quit a safe engineering job because a cog in a big wheel never sees the reward of its own creativity.
ideas.detail: His plan at 22 was to stay forever and put 15% into a 401(k) to escape his parents' turbulence. When the international group he joined grew from 7 to ~800 people in three years, his job narrowed; he built a startup on the side and quit once it had traction.

ideas.idea: Watching his father's under-capitalized, over-leveraged businesses collapse in the first storm taught him to build resilience and focus on the downside while going for the upside.
ideas.detail: His father was excellent at identifying and scaling opportunities but too aggressive; Pabrai deliberately built more resilience into his own businesses.

ideas.idea: His net worth peaked at $84M in June 2007 and bottomed under $20M in the GFC, but with no leverage and a modest lifestyle it did not change his life.
ideas.detail: He was selling stocks at a P/E of 4 to buy stocks at a P/E of 2. In 2009 the Pabrai funds rose 110-130%, nearly doubling his net worth from the bottom, followed by several strong years.

ideas.idea: The GFC's real threat was to Dakshana, funded solely by his pledge of 2% of net worth above $50M, so he cut the 2009 batch from 400 kids to 50 instead of pausing.
ideas.detail: Dakshana was spending ~$1.5M a year with hundreds of kids in IIT prep and a JV with the government of India. Officials in the Ministry of Human Resource Development advised reducing scale rather than eliminating the program because restarting would be hard; the 2010 batch was back to a normal 400.

ideas.idea: Charlie Munger never looked back at his achievements; all his energy went into the problem in front of him, and that forward focus is a better mental model than dwelling on past success.
ideas.detail: Days after Munger died at 99.9, Pabrai recalls him moaning about Berkshire's excess cash and his search for a Daily Journal CEO successor rather than discussing his legacy over 14 years of bridge and dinners. His father's prayer-corner quote: 'Success is not a summit or a peak; anything you do can be done better.'

ideas.idea: Luck plays a big role in everything good that happens in life, so he does not think in terms of success but of the next problem or milestone.
ideas.detail: Right place, right time, right people; he directs all energy to what comes next.

ideas.idea: In 2009 his worry was not his own wealth but that investors would exit at the bottom, because once they leave you can never make it back for them.
ideas.detail: The funds were down ~65% from peak versus ~40% for the index; thankfully exits were limited.

ideas.idea: A spreadsheet of what each holding is worth versus its quoted price became his rope out of the well in 2009, just as an astrologer was his bankrupt father's rope.
ideas.detail: When Pabrai was 10 or 11 in Bandra, his rational engineer father knowingly paid an orange-robed astrologer for rosy forecasts because he needed energy to start the next business. Spending more time on intrinsic values than market prices kept a sensible outlook.

ideas.idea: Use Buffett's inner scorecard: fawning and criticism both have little impact if you hold a realistic, holistic view of your own good, bad and ugly.
ideas.detail: Buffett's test: would you rather be the greatest lover known as the worst, or the worst known as the greatest? People criticize Gandhi, Buffett, Munger, even Jesus; he is a lowlife by comparison, so he learns from critics where he can and otherwise ignores them.

ideas.idea: The $2,000 industrial-psychologist assessment in 1999 was among the best money he ever spent because it gave him a map of his hard-coded inner self to align his life with.
ideas.detail: The further you are from alignment with who you are inside, the less happiness and effectiveness you have; perfectly aligned people like Buffett, Munger, Gates, Jobs and Musk can go through brick walls. After 24 years he is closer but still not fully aligned, and the payoffs of getting closer are exponential.

ideas.idea: Deliberately audit every activity, person and place for enjoyment, then increase what you liked and push down what you did not; done for decades, life becomes blissful.
ideas.detail: After 35+ years of bridge he returned to live tournaments (Chicago, Atlanta) and concluded he must play with partners much better than him to keep improving; he will attend the Louisville national only if he can find such a team.

ideas.idea: Happiness does not correlate much with wealth beyond a base level like a roof over your head; the best things in life are free.
ideas.detail: If people spent more time thinking about what would make them happier and took deliberate action, they would get there.
